paper: Carpi et al. 2021 — Comprehensive pan-genome analysis of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum complete genomes (JAM 132:592–604, doi:10.1111/jam.15199)

questions.q: Do L. plantarum ecotype/niche-specific accessory gene signatures cleanly separate food-fermentation, plant-associated, and gut/probiotic isolates within the 16k-family pan-genome, and if so, which shell/cloud gene modules are the dominant discriminators?
questions.basis: The replicated pan-genome (16,522 families; ~12.8k cloud + ~1.8k shell) is dominated by accessory content that our replication confirms is Heaps'-open (γ = 0.385). Carpi 2021 refines L. plantarum taxonomy but did not stratify openness or accessory-fraction composition by isolation source. With ~78% cloud fraction, source-metadata-conditioned structure inside shell/cloud is the natural unanswered question and is the biological engine behind the 'open pan-genome' finding.
next_steps: Recover per-genome BioSample source metadata (isolation_source, host, geo_loc) from NCBI for all 124 replication genomes and tag each of the 16,522 Roary clusters with source-frequency vectors.
Run Scoary or a permutation-based GWAS on gene_presence_absence.csv with source labels as the phenotype; correct for phylogeny using the Parsnp core-SNP tree.
Rebuild rarefaction curves stratified by source (food vs plant vs gut vs unknown) and refit Heaps' Law within each stratum to test whether openness is uniform or driven by one niche.
Cross-check top discriminating clusters against COG/KEGG functional annotation to see if food isolates over-carry EPS/plasmid genes vs plant isolates over-carrying plant-cell-wall CAZymes.

questions.q: Which subset of the 75 probiotic marker genes (PMGs) actually predicts in vitro/in vivo probiotic performance, versus being taxonomically ubiquitous ‘presence-only’ markers that carry no strain-selection signal?
questions.basis: Carpi 2021 claims ~70% of the 75 PMGs sit in core/soft-core — this is the paper's central probiotic-annotation finding, and it is exactly the claim (C4) our replication could NOT test because Wiley Cloudflare blocks the supplementary Table S5 with the PMG list. If ~70% are core/soft-core, they are by definition present in nearly every L. plantarum genome and therefore have low discriminative power for probiotic strain selection — a tension the paper does not resolve.
next_steps: Obtain the 75-PMG list (via corresponding author, ORCID contact, or PMC full-text supplementary if mirrored), cross to our gene_presence_absence.csv, and independently verify the ~70% core/soft-core fraction.

For the accessory-fraction PMGs (the ~30% that are strain-variable), test correlation with published in vitro probiotic phenotypes (bile-salt tolerance, adhesion, antimicrobial activity) using strains in the paper's cohort that have phenotypic data (e.g. WCFS1, LP-115).
Build a compact 'informative-PMG' panel (probably 10–20 genes) whose accessory-fraction status carries actual predictive signal and propose it as an updated screening marker set.
Compare informative-PMG panel against a null model of randomly drawn shell-fraction genes to establish effect size vs baseline.

questions.q: Where does the L. plantarum / L. pentosus / L. paraplantarum species boundary actually sit under a modern genomic species concept (ANI ≥ 95% and/or dDDH ≥ 70% and/or core-genome tree topology), and how many of the 127/124 'complete L. plantarum' genomes are edge cases that would be reclassified?
questions.basis: Carpi 2021 uses FastANI as a sanity check but does not systematically report ANI/dDDH matrices for the boundary with L. pentosus and L. paraplantarum, the two closest relatives that are known to be routinely misannotated in RefSeq. Our replication inherited three RefSeq-dropped genomes (CNEI-KCA5, KLDS1.0391, SN13T) — hinting that RefSeq curation itself struggles with this boundary. This is directly the 'refine taxonomy' half of the paper's aim, only partially discharged.
next_steps: Run FastANI all-vs-all on our 124 genomes plus all NCBI complete L. pentosus (~40) and L. paraplantarum (~15) as outgroups; produce the full ANI matrix.
Compute dDDH with GGDC 3.0 (or SkANI + a dDDH proxy) for any pair with ANI in 94–96% (boundary zone).
Reconstruct a core-genome tree with Parsnp restricted to shared L. plantarum/pentosus/paraplantarum core and test whether any of the 124 sit inside the L. pentosus clade under maximum-likelihood.
Report an audit list of L. plantarum genomes that should be reclassified and propose corrections back to NCBI via the Genome-Assembly BioProject curation channel.

questions.q: How much of the L. plantarum pan-genome openness (γ = 0.385) is driven by plasmid- and mobile-genetic-element (MGE) content rather than chromosomal accessory genes, and does the plasmidome alone show a Heaps' exponent statistically distinguishable from the chromosome?
questions.basis: Carpi 2021 counts plasmids/prophages/CRISPR/bacteriocins as downstream analyses but does not decompose Heaps' openness into plasmid vs chromosomal contributions. LAB (lactic-acid bacteria) are known for large plasmidomes with heavy horizontal transfer, and the paper's 78% cloud fraction is a red flag for MGE dominance. Our replication reproduced the openness result without addressing this decomposition — the mechanism behind γ = 0.385 remains unresolved.
next_steps: Split each of the 124 assemblies into chromosomal vs plasmid contigs using MOB-suite / PlasmidFinder / Platon; recompute Roary independently on {chromosome-only} and {plasmid-only} FASTA sets.
Refit Heaps' Law on each stratum; test γ_chr vs γ_plasmid with bootstrap CIs (500 permutations of genome order).
Cross accessory clusters against Mobile Genetic Element databases (ICEberg, ISfinder, PHASTER prophage regions) and quantify the MGE-annotated fraction of the shell + cloud partition.
If plasmid/MGE fraction dominates openness, quantify per-plasmid replicon-family (repA typing) frequencies to test whether specific replicon lineages are responsible for the accessory bloom.

questions.q: How does the core-vs-accessory split of fermentation-central metabolism (EMP glycolysis, phosphoketolase / PPP branching, mannitol production, exopolysaccharide biosynthesis, plantaricin bacteriocin clusters) map across the 124-genome pan-genome, and which industrial-strain design choices are constrained by accessory-fraction pathway modules?
questions.basis: Carpi 2021's motivation is 'probiotic and industrial application' but the paper reports pan-genome architecture at the family-count level without a systematic core/accessory annotation of the metabolic modules that actually differentiate L. plantarum industrial strains (EPS diversity, mannitol vs lactate flux, plantaricin gene-cluster completeness). Our replication provides the substrate (gene_presence_absence.csv with 16,522 clusters) but did not map fermentation pathways onto it — a natural downstream question the paper leaves open.
next_steps: Annotate the 16,522 Roary clusters with KEGG KO IDs via eggNOG-mapper or DIAMOND vs UniRef90 → KEGG.

Map KOs to KEGG modules for glycolysis (map00010), PPP (map00030), fructose/mannose (map00051, mannitol dehydrogenase mtlD), EPS biosynthesis (map00541), and bacteriocin ORF clusters (plnABCD via BAGEL4).
Compute per-module completeness scores per genome; classify each module as 'core-complete' (present in ≥99% strains) vs 'accessory-variable'.

For the accessory-variable modules (likely EPS + plantaricin), cluster strains by module presence pattern and cross-reference to reported industrial phenotype (yogurt / vegetable-ferment / silage / probiotic) to build a strain-selection lookup for a target product.
